case_mappings.clinical_pattern: A 45-year-old woman has recurrent aching pain in the right wrist and MCP joints of both hands, mild joint swelling, morning stiffness and functional difficulty. She reports nocturnal tingling/numbness in the right thumb and index finger. Examination shows swelling/tenderness at the wrist, MCP and PIP joints, reduced sensation in the right thumb/index, but normal muscle power and no thenar wasting. Small painless subcutaneous nodules are present near the elbow. Hand/wrist X-rays show periarticular soft-tissue swelling and periarticular osteopenia; ESR is raised, mild hypochromic normocytic anemia and positive rheumatoid factor are reported. Nerve conduction shows reduced velocity in the right median nerve distal to the wrist. The PBL diagnosis is Rheumatoid Arthritis.
case_mappings.most_relevant_topic: Rheumatoid Arthritis with associated right median nerve compression / carpal tunnel syndrome features. The case explicitly diagnoses RA and reports slowed median nerve conduction distal to the wrist.

anatomy_links.topic: Median nerve sensory territory in the hand and carpal tunnel compression
Flexor retinaculum, carpal tunnel and flexor synovial sheaths
Thenar muscles and recurrent median nerve branch (LOAF)

clinical_correlation: Bilateral MCP/PIP and wrist symptoms with morning stiffness, swelling and raised ESR support an inflammatory polyarthritis pattern; the supplied PBL names Rheumatoid Arthritis.
Numbness/tingling in the thumb and index finger, especially at night, together with reduced median nerve conduction distal to the wrist, indicates median nerve involvement at the wrist.
No thenar wasting and normal motor power are documented; do not add thenar atrophy to this patient's findings.
Subcutaneous nodules near the elbow are a systemic extra-articular clue described in the case.

The PBL states an indomethacin dose as '150 gm/day'; this is an apparent source-unit error and must not be treated as a usable prescription. The source later describes methotrexate 7.5 mg weekly and physiotherapy.
source_notes: The source text inconsistently calls the patient Qesmah and later Farida; the JSON retains Qesmah, the name used in the case opening.
The printed indomethacin unit is 'gm/day' and is clearly unsafe/implausible as written; retained only as a flagged transcription issue, not clinical advice.

case_mappings.clinical_pattern: A 55-year-old male painter has hand and wrist pain with tingling, occasional sharp shooting pain extending from the wrist up the arm during work, weak grip, difficulty grasping small objects and wasting at the base of the thumb. He has had diabetes mellitus for 10 years.
case_mappings.most_relevant_topic: Carpal Tunnel Syndrome (median nerve compression in the carpal tunnel), as indicated by the case questions and thenar wasting; diabetes is a risk factor to consider.

anatomy_links.topic: Carpal tunnel formed by the carpal arch and flexor retinaculum
Median nerve sensory territory and thenar motor supply
Thenar muscles and recurrent branch of median nerve

clinical_correlation: Median nerve compression can cause pain/tingling in its hand sensory territory and weakness/wasting of thenar muscles in more advanced disease.
The palmar cutaneous branch passes superficial to the flexor retinaculum, so sensation over the thenar eminence is typically spared in carpal tunnel syndrome.
The case asks about diagnosis, causes, symptoms, risk groups and treatment; it does not provide test results or a confirmed treatment plan.

case_mappings.clinical_pattern: A volleyball player injures the index finger. There is immediate pain and swelling at the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joint, a sensation that something gave way, drooping of the fingertip and inability to actively extend the DIP joint. The case identifies the condition as Mallet finger.
case_mappings.most_relevant_topic: Mallet finger due to disruption of the terminal extensor mechanism at the DIP joint; assess for associated avulsion fracture and joint alignment as appropriate.

anatomy_links.topic: Dorsal extensor expansion and terminal extensor slips
Finger extensor apparatus and intrinsic muscle contributions

clinical_correlation: The defining finding in the case is inability to actively extend the DIP joint with a drooping fingertip.
The source asks how to confirm the diagnosis and what other problems may coexist, but it does not provide the answers or imaging findings.

case_mappings.case: Hook of hamate fracture / Guyon canal compression
case_mappings.clinical_pattern: A racket-sport or golf player may fracture the hook of hamate; ulnar nerve compression can occur in Guyon canal near the pisiform and hook of hamate.
case_mappings.most_relevant_topic: Hook of hamate injury and ulnar nerve entrapment in Guyon canal.

anatomy_links.topic: Hook of hamate and Guyon canal
Ulnar nerve entrapment in Guyon canal

clinical_correlation: The hand lecture links hook of hamate fracture to racket sports and golf and describes ulnar nerve compression in Guyon canal.
The nerve-injury lecture lists hook of hamate fracture and Guyon canal syndrome as wrist-level ulnar nerve injury contexts.

case_mappings.clinical_pattern: Progressive fibrosis and degeneration of palmar fascia/aponeurosis, affecting digits 4 and 5 most often.
case_mappings.most_relevant_topic: Dupuytren contracture; distinguish it from ulnar claw hand and rheumatoid/intrinsic joint disease using the lecture's comparison.
clinical_correlation: The lecture states digits 4 and 5 are most affected and males are affected more often.

Its differential comparison notes that in ulnar nerve palsy there may be intrinsic muscle wasting and sensory loss, while the fingers can still be passively straightened; RA/intrinsic joint disease has joint pain, swelling, morning stiffness and erosive X-ray changes.

case_mappings.clinical_pattern: Median nerve injury at the elbow may cause loss of pronation, weak flexion, benediction hand when attempting to make a fist, loss of FPL function/negative OK sign, and thenar weakness. Injury at the wrist can produce thenar wasting and loss of opposition/abduction.
case_mappings.most_relevant_topic: Median nerve lesion level and clinical signs; carpal tunnel syndrome is a compression neuropathy at the wrist.

anatomy_links.topic: Median nerve motor/sensory distribution and lesion patterns

clinical_correlation: Benediction hand is described in the source when attempting to make a fist after median nerve injury at the elbow.
Ape-like hand reflects thenar muscle paralysis/wasting and loss of opposition/abduction.
Carpal tunnel syndrome typically spares sensation over the thenar eminence because the palmar cutaneous branch passes superficial to the flexor retinaculum.

case_mappings.clinical_pattern: Ulnar nerve injury at or above the elbow produces partial clawing most prominent in digits 4 and 5, interosseous wasting and altered thumb position. A wrist/hand lesion may produce more marked clawing (ulnar paradox).
case_mappings.most_relevant_topic: Ulnar nerve motor supply to intrinsic hand muscles, PAD/DAB actions, and lesion-level differences.

anatomy_links.topic: Ulnar nerve motor branches and sensory territory
Hypothenar, adductor pollicis, lumbricals and interossei

clinical_correlation: Ulnar nerve supplies all interossei, hypothenar muscles, adductor pollicis and medial two lumbricals in the hand, as listed in the lecture.
PAD = palmar interossei adduct; DAB = dorsal interossei abduct.
The source describes ulnar paradox: a distal lesion can cause more obvious clawing because the medial half of FDP remains innervated.

case_mappings.clinical_pattern: Radial nerve injury may follow crutch palsy, Saturday night palsy, humeral shaft fracture or supracondylar fracture; motor findings include finger drop and wrist drop.
case_mappings.most_relevant_topic: Radial nerve motor supply and sensory territory on the dorsum of the hand.

anatomy_links.topic: Radial nerve branches and injury findings

clinical_correlation: The lecture describes sensory loss limited by overlap to a small triangular area on the dorsum near the base of the thumb/first dorsal interosseous space.
The lecture lists finger drop and wrist drop as motor deformities.

osce_framework.title: Focused Hand and Wrist Examination
osce_framework.status: Generated study framework; not an official university station.
steps: Introduce yourself, confirm patient identity, explain the examination and obtain consent.
Inspect both hands and wrists: swelling, erythema, deformity, scars, skin changes, thenar/hypothenar wasting, interosseous wasting and finger posture.
Assess active and passive range of motion of wrist, MCP, PIP and DIP joints; compare sides and note pain/stiffness.
Assess grip and pinch strength; test thumb opposition, abduction, adduction and flexion.
Test median nerve: sensation over palmar lateral 3½ fingers; thenar motor function; consider Phalen-type wrist flexion and Tinel tapping if carpal tunnel is suspected.
Test ulnar nerve: sensation over medial 1½ fingers; finger abduction/adduction (interossei), Froment-type pinch and hypothenar function.
Test radial nerve: wrist, finger and thumb extension; assess dorsal first web-space sensation.
Assess circulation: radial/ulnar pulses, capillary refill, temperature and colour.
Examine relevant joints and systemic features when inflammatory arthritis is suspected; document findings and compare both hands.
Thank the patient, ensure comfort and summarize findings.
clinical_focus: Carpal tunnel syndrome: median nerve symptoms, thenar function and sensory sparing over thenar eminence.
Ulnar neuropathy: interossei weakness, sensory change in medial 1½ fingers and clawing.
Radial neuropathy: wrist/finger extension weakness and dorsal hand sensory territory.
Mallet finger: inspect DIP droop and test active DIP extension; avoid forceful movement if acutely painful.

quality_notes: Case mappings distinguish the formal Main PBL (Qesmah) and two complementary cases (Jasim and Salam) from applied anatomy clinical correlations drawn from the lecture slides.

The PBL explicitly diagnoses Qesmah with Rheumatoid Arthritis and reports reduced right median nerve conduction distal to the wrist; carpal tunnel syndrome is a relevant associated clinical interpretation, not the named primary PBL diagnosis.
The PBL uses the name Qesmah in the opening and later refers to her as Farida. This inconsistency is flagged rather than silently reconciled.
The PBL prints 'indomethacin capsules 150 gm/day'. This is an apparent source-unit error and is not reproduced as a usable treatment recommendation. Do not use this as clinical dosing guidance.
The complementary cases explicitly name Carpal Tunnel Syndrome in the Jasim question set and Mallet finger in Salam's case narrative; they do not provide answers to their question prompts.

The supplied PBL has actual hand radiographs on PDF page 2: a normal hand image and a rheumatoid arthritis image labelled with bone erosion and bone displacement. No image is embedded in the complementary-case PDF.
Anatomy of hand PDF pages 36, 38–43, 45, 47 and 48 are primarily visual slides with little/no extractable text; they were inspected visually and included in the image inventory where useful.
